# Getting Data In: Files {#sec-acquisition}

```{r}
#| label: acq-opening
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
opening_base <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"))
opening_readr <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                          col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
opening_rand <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                         col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
opening_zeros <- sum(as.character(opening_base$patient_id) !=
                       opening_readr$patient_id)
opening_orphans <- nrow(anti_join(opening_readr, opening_rand,
                                  by = "patient_id"))
```

Every data chapter after this one begins with a data frame already
in memory, as though it had arrived there by itself. It did not.
Read the HF-HOME case report form (CRF) export with base R's
`read.csv()`, and `r format(opening_zeros, big.mark = ",")` of
`r format(nrow(opening_base), big.mark = ",")` patient identifiers
lose their leading zeros; read it with `readr`, and the zeros
survive everywhere except in the `r opening_orphans` identifiers
that one site's system had already stripped before the file was
written. Neither reader warns, and a join to a randomization list
that kept its zeros drops every one of those patients. A value
that is silently misread at import is a value that no downstream
test will catch, which is why this chapter treats getting data in
as the first step of the analysis rather than a preamble to it.


  compute what the default read got wrong.
- Detect the file pathologies of a clinical export (byte-order
  mark, line endings, lost leading zeros, missing-value codes,
  per-site formats) and write an assertion for each.

## Three ways data arrive {#sec-acquisition-routes}

Data arrive as a file, through an interface, or off a web page,
and the three differ in how much control you have over what
arrives (@tbl-acquisition-routes). A **file** is a snapshot someone
made for you; its pathologies are all present the moment you
receive it. An **interface**, such as the application programming
interface (API) of REDCap or of an institutional data warehouse, is
a query against a living system, so the code is deterministic and
the data source is not. A **scrape** is what you resort to when the
data exist but no interface does. This chapter reads files;
@sec-apis takes up interfaces and pages.

| Source | What can go wrong | What you control | How to freeze it |
|---|---|---|---|
| File | Encoding, line endings, delimiter, guessed column types, missing-value codes | Only how you read it | Keep the file as received, read-only, with a checksum |
| Interface | Authentication, pagination, rate limits, a response shape that changes without notice | The query | Write each response to a dated raw file with a provenance note |
| Web page | Terms of use, page structure that is not a contract, personal data | The selector, and whether to scrape at all | Save the page or the parsed table, dated, once |

: The three routes by which data arrive. The last column is the
same discipline in three forms. {#tbl-acquisition-routes}

The routes differ in almost everything except their ending, and
@fig-acquisition-routes puts them side by side because the checking
step they converge on is the step most often skipped.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-acquisition-routes
%%| fig-alt: "Three source nodes converging on one. A file raises
%%|   delimiter, encoding and column-type problems; an interface
%%|   raises authentication, pagination, rate limits and JSON shape;
%%|   a web page raises terms of use, selectors and silent structure
%%|   changes. All three lead to a single checked analysis file with
%%|   types asserted, levels counted and missingness described,
%%|   which then feeds everything downstream."
%%| fig-cap: "The three ways data arrive and the one step they
%%|   share. A file, an interface, and a web page raise different
%%|   problems on the way in, but all three produce an object that
%%|   must be checked before anything downstream can be trusted."
flowchart TD
  F["<b>A file</b><br/><i>delimiter, encoding,<br/>column types</i>"]
  A["<b>An interface</b><br/><i>authentication, pagination,<br/>rate limits, JSON shape</i>"]
  W["<b>A web page</b><br/><i>terms of use, selectors,<br/>silent structure changes</i>"]
  F --> C["<b>Checked analysis file</b><br/><i>types asserted, levels counted,<br/>missingness described</i>"]
  A --> C
  W --> C
  C --> D["Everything downstream<br/><i>wrangling, joining, modeling</i>"]
```

### The raw-data rule

The three routes converge on a single discipline, the **raw-data
rule**: the data as received are read-only, and every change to
them lives in a script rather than in the file (Habit 2). At the
acquisition step the rule has a second clause: whatever you
acquire, write it down, date it, and never acquire it again in the
same breath as analyzing it. @sec-wrangling applies the same rule
to cleaning.

The rule follows from treating acquisition as a step rather than a
preamble. The instinct is to regard 'getting the data' as something
that happens before the analysis starts, and therefore something
that need not be scripted to the same standard. This is backwards.
The acquisition determines which rows exist, and no amount of care
downstream can recover a row that was silently dropped at import.
The script that acquires is the first script in the pipeline and
is held to the same standard as the last.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A collaborator opens the CRF export in a spreadsheet,
fixes three obviously wrong site labels by hand, saves it, and
sends it back. The fixes are correct. What has been lost?

**Answer.** The evidence. The file you hold is no longer the file
the sites produced, nothing records which three cells changed or
why, and the next export from the sites will arrive with the same
three errors and no script to correct them. The spreadsheet may
also have rewritten other cells on save, for example by stripping
leading zeros from identifiers. Under the raw-data rule the
collaborator's three corrections become three lines in the
cleaning script, run against the untouched export.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Ethics'}
Before assembling data from several routes, ask whether the
people in it would be surprised to find their records joined.
Linking sources that are each harmless can create a profile none
of them disclosed; @sec-ethics-aggregation works through the
argument, and @sec-apis applies it to scraping.
:::

## Reading files deliberately {#sec-acquisition-files}

The tidyverse import story is one function per format:
`readr::read_csv()` and its relatives for delimited text,
`readxl::read_excel()` for spreadsheets, `haven::read_sas()` and
`haven::read_xpt()` for the SAS world of @sec-sas. They share an
interface and a philosophy: they parse, they report what they did,
and they fail loudly if you tell them what to expect. The generic
tour is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, ch. 7]; this
section reads one real export.

### The default read

The HF-HOME CRF export, `crf_export.csv`, holds one row per
patient from five hospitals, each of which wrote its own
conventions into the file (the codebook is `README.md` beside it).
Read it twice with the defaults, once with base R and once with
`readr`:

```{r}
#| label: acq-naive
library(tidyverse)
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
crf_path <- file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv")

naive_base  <- read.csv(crf_path)
naive_readr <- read_csv(crf_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

str(naive_base[, c("patient_id", "dob", "sbp_discharge")])
spec(naive_readr)
```

Both reads succeed in silence, and both are wrong in ways the
output does not show. `read.csv()` made the identifier an integer,
so `0007` is now `7`. `readr` kept it as text, a property of
`readr`'s guesser and not of R, and relying on it is a mistake: the
day a collaborator uses `read.csv()`, or the file arrives through
`readxl`, the zeros go. Both readers left the dates as text and
read Site D's missing-value code, `-99`, as a blood pressure.

### The specified read

The remedy is to say what you expect. A full column specification
names every column's type, and the `na` argument names every
string that means 'missing':

```{r}
#| label: acq-spec
crf_spec <- cols(
  patient_id     = col_character(),
  site           = col_character(),
  sex            = col_character(),
  dob            = col_character(),
  discharge_date = col_character(),
  ef_pct         = col_double(),
  sbp_discharge  = col_double(),
  weight_kg      = col_double()
)
crf <- read_csv(crf_path, col_types = crf_spec,
                na = c("", "NA", "-99"))
problems(crf)
```

The dates stay as text on purpose. The sites wrote them in four
formats, and a `col_date()` here would be a promise the file cannot
keep; @sec-wrangling parses them site by site. One `na` list
applies to every column, which is safe here only because no
identifier or label in this file can legitimately read `-99`; the
assertions below check that assumption.

The difference between the reads is a computation, not an
impression:

```{r}
#| label: acq-diffs
iso_date <- "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$"
read_diffs <- tibble(
  column = c("patient_id", "patient_id", "sbp_discharge",
             "weight_kg", "discharge_date", "site"),
  problem = c("leading zeros dropped by read.csv()",
              "leading zeros already missing in the file",
              "-99 read as a pressure by both default reads",
              "-99 read as a weight by both default reads",
              "not in ISO 8601 form",
              "distinct spellings of five sites"),
  rows = c(
    sum(as.character(naive_base$patient_id) != crf$patient_id),
    sum(nchar(crf$patient_id) < 4),
    sum(naive_readr$sbp_discharge == -99, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(naive_readr$weight_kg == -99, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(!str_detect(crf$discharge_date, iso_date)),
    n_distinct(crf$site)
  )
)
read_diffs
```

The specification repairs what a read can repair: the identifier
stays text and the missing-value code becomes `NA`. The last four
rows are facts about the file, which no reader can fix and a
cleaning script must. The `r read_diffs$rows[2]` short identifiers
are the ones Site E's system stripped before export; restoring them
with `str_pad()` is safe only because the codebook says every
identifier has four digits (@sec-wrangling).

A specification is also an assertion. Declare the discharge date as
an ISO 8601 date, which the codebook promises for the clean tables
but not for this export, and `readr` says so, row by row:

```{r}
#| label: acq-strict
#| warning: true
strict_spec <- crf_spec
strict_spec$cols$discharge_date <- col_date()
strict <- read_csv(crf_path, col_types = strict_spec,
                   na = c("", "NA", "-99"))
nrow(problems(strict))
strict |>
  count(site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)),
        unparsed = is.na(discharge_date))
```

Every failure is at Sites C, D, and E, the three that do not write
ISO dates. When next month's extract changes, a full specification
turns the change into a warning and a `problems()` table naming the
row, the column, and what was expected, rather than a data frame
that is quietly different from last month's. An empty `problems()`
table is a passed assertion; inspect it after every read.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Whether an identifier survives depends on which reader you
call.** `readr` guesses `patient_id` as text here only because
some values have leading zeros in its sample. `read.csv()`,
`data.table::fread()`, and a spreadsheet opened and re-saved all
make it a number. Two files read by coercing readers then join
without error on integers, the row count is right, and every
identifier that carried a leading zero no longer matches the
source system. Write `col_character()` for every identifier, on
every read of a file you did not create.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to draft the specification, from the codebook rather
than from the data.

> **Context.** I am reading `crf_export.csv`, a raw CRF export from
> five sites. Its header and the codebook entries for each column
> are below, followed by three synthetic rows I made up in the
> file's format. The identifier is four digits with leading zeros.
>
> **Constraints.** Use `readr::read_csv()` with a complete `cols()`
> specification, every column named, no `.default`. Identifiers are
> `col_character()`. Keep any column whose format varies by site as
> character. Declare the missing-value codes the codebook lists in
> `na`.
>
> **Criteria.** Justify each column's type in one line, citing the
> codebook. List every assumption you made that the codebook does
> not state. Write a `stopifnot()` that fails if the identifier is
> not character or if any numeric column holds a value outside a
> range you state.

*Failure mode.* A model infers types from the rows it sees, exactly
as `read_csv()` does, so it inherits the guesser's blindness: shown
rows without leading zeros, it makes the identifier an integer, and
shown no `-99`, it omits the code. *Check.* Run the read, then
`problems()`, then the checks in @sec-acquisition-checks; compare
the model's `na` list with the missing-value table in
@sec-wrangling. Send the codebook and synthetic rows, never the
export (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Pathologies that do not announce themselves {#sec-acquisition-pathologies}

Two more properties of this file are invisible on screen. Its first
three bytes are a UTF-8 **byte-order mark** (BOM), and every line
ends in a carriage return and a line feed (CRLF), the Windows
convention. @sec-shell shows both at the byte level. What they do
depends on the reader and on the machine, and the claims commonly
made about them are too strong. Compare three reads:

```{r}
#| label: acq-bom
readBin(crf_path, "raw", n = 3)

c(
  `read_csv()` = names(naive_readr)[1],
  `read.csv(), UTF-8 locale` = names(naive_base)[1],
  `read.csv(), C locale` = withr::with_locale(
    c(LC_CTYPE = "C"), names(read.csv(crf_path))[1]
  )
)
```

`readr` removes the mark, and so does base R's `read.csv()` in a
UTF-8 locale, the default on current macOS, Windows, and most Linux
desktops. In the C (POSIX) locale, which R falls back to in a
container or on a server where no locale has been set,
`read.csv()` keeps the three
bytes and `check.names` turns them into dots, so the first column is
`X...patient_id` and `x$patient_id` returns `NULL`.[^bom-readers]
The same script then works on your laptop and fails, or worse
returns `NULL` into a check, in the container.

[^bom-readers]: As run for this edition (R 4.6.1, `readr` 2.2.0,
    `data.table` 1.18.4, macOS): `data.table::fread()` also removes
    the mark. Python's `csv` module keeps it when the file is opened
    with `encoding='utf-8'`, so the first name is
    `'\ufeffpatient_id'`, and removes it with `encoding='utf-8-sig'`.
    Shell tools keep it (@sec-shell).

The carriage returns are harmless to every R reader shown here,
which accept either line ending. They matter at the shell, where
`cut` and `grep` see a `\r` at the end of every last field, and in
any parser you write yourself.

@tbl-import-checklist collects the file pathologies of this export
and three that it happens not to have, with how each shows itself
and the assertion that makes it loud.

| Pathology | Symptom | Detection | Fix | Assertion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Byte-order mark | First column name changes with the reader and locale | `readBin(f, "raw", 3)` is `ef bb bf` | `read_csv()`, or `fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM"` | `names(x)[1] == "patient_id"` |
| CRLF line endings | `\r` on the last field, at the shell | `od -c`, `cat -e` (@sec-shell) | None needed in R; never edit the raw file | Last numeric column parses with no `problems()` |
| Leading zeros lost | `7` where the key is `0007`; joins drop patients | `count(x, nchar(patient_id))` | `col_character()`; `str_pad()` only by the codebook | `all(nchar(x$patient_id) == 4)` |
| Missing-value codes | `-99` averaged as a pressure | Count codes by site (@sec-wrangling) | `na = c("", "NA", "-99")` | `all(between(x$sbp, 50, 250), na.rm = TRUE)` |
| Formats by site | Dates stay text; a single parse misreads some | `count(x, site, str_detect(d, iso))` | Character at read; parse per site (@sec-types) | `!anyNA(date)` after parsing |
| Label variants | Fifteen spellings of five sites | `count(x, site)` | `str_squish()`, `str_to_title()` | `all(site %in% expected)` |
| Wrong delimiter | One wide column | `ncol(x)` | `read_tsv()` or `delim =` | `ncol(x) == 8` |
| Wrong encoding | `Z\xfcrich` for Zürich | `stringi::stri_enc_isutf8()` | `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")` | All strings valid UTF-8 |
| Excel serial dates | Five-digit numbers in a date column | A date-named column that is numeric | `janitor::excel_numeric_to_date()` (@sec-types) | Dates within the study period |

: The import checklist. The first six rows are planted in the
HF-HOME export; the last three are common elsewhere.
{#tbl-import-checklist}

### Checking as an artifact, not an activity {#sec-acquisition-checks}

Every analyst checks data. The question is whether anyone can see
that they did. A check run at the console leaves nothing behind: it
is not re-run when the extract is refreshed, and a reviewer cannot
tell which pathologies were looked for. Harrell's *R Workflow*
[@harrell2025rworkflow] makes data checking and data overview
numbered chapters of the workflow, with their output a section of
the rendered report. What makes a check trustworthy is that it
lives in the document, so it executes on every render and fails
loudly when the next extract violates an assumption the first one
satisfied.

In the tidyverse idiom, the artifact is a function that returns one
result per row of the checklist, applied to each read:

```{r}
#| label: acq-checks
randomization <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                          col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

check_import <- function(x) {
  c(
    header       = identical(names(x)[1], "patient_id"),
    rows         = nrow(x) == nrow(randomization),
    id_is_text   = is.character(x$patient_id),
    id_width_4   = all(nchar(as.character(x$patient_id)) == 4),
    id_unique    = !anyDuplicated(x$patient_id),
    sbp_range    = all(between(x$sbp_discharge, 50, 250),
                       na.rm = TRUE),
    weight_range = all(between(x$weight_kg, 30, 250), na.rm = TRUE),
    site_labels  = all(x$site %in% paste("Site", LETTERS[1:5]))
  )
}

tibble(
  check     = names(check_import(crf)),
  read.csv  = check_import(naive_base),
  readr     = check_import(naive_readr),
  specified = check_import(crf)
)
```

The specified read passes every check a read can pass. The two
failures it keeps, the identifier width and the site labels, are
the repairs @sec-wrangling makes; the import script records them
and asserts that they are confined to where the codebook says they
are, so that a new kind of failure stops the build.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The build-time form of the checks is a `stopifnot()` that prints
nothing when the file is as expected:

```{r}
#| label: acq-verify
crf_checks <- check_import(crf)
short_id_sites <- crf |>
  filter(nchar(patient_id) < 4) |>
  distinct(site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)))

stopifnot(
  all(crf_checks[c("header", "rows", "id_is_text", "id_unique",
                   "sbp_range", "weight_range")]),
  identical(short_id_sites$site, "Site E"),
  nrow(problems(crf)) == 0
)
```

If Site B's system begins dropping zeros next quarter, the second
assertion fails and names the change, instead of the join in
@sec-joins quietly losing Site B's patients.
:::

`skimr::skim()` and `count()` belong beside the assertions: `skim()`
reports what each column looks like, and `count()` exposes the level
the codebook did not mention. The first two are for the reader; the
`stopifnot()` is for the build. @sec-testing develops the assertion
side into a test suite.

### Exercises

1. Using `crf` from the specified read, count by site the patients
   whose `patient_id` matches no row of `randomization.csv`. Pad the
   identifiers to four digits and show that the anti-join is then
   empty.
2. Add two checks to `check_import()`: one that fails when the
   columns are not exactly those in the codebook, in order, and one
   that fails when any numeric column holds the value `-99`. Report
   the result for all three reads.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-12b-1
crf |>
  anti_join(randomization, by = "patient_id") |>
  count(site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)))

padded <- crf |>
  mutate(patient_id = str_pad(patient_id, width = 4, pad = "0"))
stopifnot(nrow(anti_join(padded, randomization,
                         by = "patient_id")) == 0)
```

Every unmatched patient is at Site E, which is the codebook's
account of the file. A join on the unpadded key would have dropped
them all without an error (@sec-joins).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-12b-2
codebook_cols <- c("patient_id", "site", "sex", "dob",
                   "discharge_date", "ef_pct", "sbp_discharge",
                   "weight_kg")

check_import_2 <- function(x) {
  numeric_cols <- c("ef_pct", "sbp_discharge", "weight_kg")
  c(
    check_import(x),
    columns = identical(names(x), codebook_cols),
    no_code = !any(vapply(numeric_cols,
                          \(v) any(x[[v]] == -99, na.rm = TRUE),
                          logical(1)))
  )
}

tibble(
  check     = names(check_import_2(crf)),
  read.csv  = check_import_2(naive_base),
  readr     = check_import_2(naive_readr),
  specified = check_import_2(crf)
) |>
  tail(2)
```

All three reads have the codebook's columns in this locale; under
the C locale `read.csv()` fails the `columns` check, because its
first name is `X...patient_id`. Only the specified read passes
`no_code`. The `-99` check is narrower than the range checks, and
that is its value: a failure names the cause, not only the symptom.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your cohort has 1,000 patients. You read the
demographics file and the visits file, both without a column
specification, join them on `patient_id`, and get 1,000 rows,
which is what you expected. What might still be wrong?

**Answer.** If one file was read by a coercing reader and the other
by `readr`, the join fails with a type error, which is the good
case. If both were read by coercing readers, both identifiers are
integers, the join succeeds, the row count is right, and every
identifier that carried a leading zero no longer matches the source
system. The analysis is internally consistent and externally wrong:
the day someone asks you to re-identify a case for a data query,
you cannot. The row count was never sensitive to the failure. Read
identifiers as character, always, and assert it.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence.** Keep what you received
   read-only and unedited, and make every change in a script run
   against the untouched file.
2. **Habit 7: convert late, validate early.** Specify every column,
   read identifiers as character, and keep site-dependent formats
   as text until a script parses them by rule.
3. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** A `-99` averaged as a pressure raises
   nothing; write the assertion for each row of the import
   checklist.

## Cumulative practice

3. *On your own work (no key).* Take a delimited file you did not
   create. Read it once with no arguments and once with a full
   column specification, compute the differences as in
   @sec-acquisition-files, and say for each disagreement which read
   is correct.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Read with a contract | `read_csv(f, col_types = cols(...), na = c("", "NA", "-99"))` | Guessed types; missing codes as data |
| Keep identifiers | `patient_id = col_character()` | Lost leading zeros |
| Read everything as text | `cols(.default = col_character())` | Conversions before you have looked |
| See parse failures | `problems(x)` | A changed extract read quietly |
| Look at the first bytes | `readBin(f, "raw", n = 3)` | Byte-order marks |
| Declare an encoding | `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")` | Mangled accented names |
| Assert the import | `stopifnot(names(x)[1] == "patient_id", ...)` | Reader and locale differences |

: Reading files at a glance. {#tbl-acquisition-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@wickham2023r4ds], the data-import and spreadsheet chapters,
  the canonical applied treatment of `readr` and `readxl`.
- [@harrell2025rworkflow], Chapters 7 and 8, on data checking and
  data overview as reported steps of the workflow. The code is
  `data.table` and `Hmisc` rather than tidyverse
  (@sec-alternative-wrangling covers the dialect), but the
  structural argument transfers intact.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-12b}

1. The guess is made from a sample (the first thousand rows by
   default), so any pathology that does not appear in the sample
   is invisible to it. Two consequences produce no error. First, a
   code used upstream to mean 'missing', such as -99, is guessed as
   a number and enters the analysis as a measurement, dragging
   every mean it touches. Second, a column of dates in an
   ambiguous or site-specific format is guessed as character and
   sorts as text, or is parsed under the wrong convention, so that
   03/04/2026 is March in one file and April in another. A third
   hazard is commonly misdescribed: whether an identifier with
   leading zeros survives depends on which reader you call.
   `readr` keeps `0007` as text when its sample shows the zeros;
   base R's `read.csv()` and most spreadsheet exports make it the
   integer 7. The remedy in every case is a full `col_types`
   specification and an explicit `na` argument, treated as
   assertions, with `problems()` checked after every read.
2. Because the file is evidence and the corrections are not
   recorded. Nothing says which cells changed or why, the next
   export will arrive with the same errors and no script to fix
   them, and the spreadsheet may have rewritten other cells on
   save, for example by stripping leading zeros. Keep the export
   as received and make the three corrections lines of the
   cleaning script.
3. Base R's `read.csv()` removes the mark in a UTF-8 locale but
   keeps it in the C (POSIX) locale that a container or server
   often falls back to. There `check.names` turns the three bytes
   into dots, the first column is named `X...patient_id`, and
   `x$patient_id` returns `NULL`. Read with `read_csv()`, which
   removes the mark in either locale, and assert
   `names(x)[1] == "patient_id"`.
